snippet: I thought I'd share a personal work experience that could be of interest to non-finance people who are still figuring out whether AI is coming for their jobs. A short🧵. 1/
content_text: [1/16 @__paleologo] I thought I'd share a personal work experience that could be of interest to non-finance people who are still figuring out whether AI is coming for their jobs. A short🧵. 1/ --- [2/16 @__paleologo] Everyone who works in fundamental and systematic equities investing has gone through at least one crowding/derisking event. Q1 2016; Q4 2018; Q1 2020; Q1 2025. And many smaller ones. Since ~2020 I have been thinking about a way to model crowding and derisking phenomena. 2/ --- [3/16 @__paleologo] Enough that in 2024, when I gave a keynote at a Fordham conference on my favorite open problems, I listed "crowding" as #2 (out of 6). 3/ --- [4/16 @__paleologo] I discussed this with friends and colleagues (I am not very secretive), but my tentative models did not even reproduce the basic dynamics of the event. Very frustrating. 4/ --- [5/16 @__paleologo] A couple of weeks ago, I revisited the model. Shared it with Sol, now with Astra, and started to discuss it. I could work out the implications much faster, and run simulations in parallel. 5/ --- [6/16 @__paleologo] Sort of amazingly, we converged to a very simple model, which, with parameters that are very reasonable, describes to the right order of magnitude the interval between event, the duration of the derisking, the duration of the recovery, and the shape of the losses. 6/ --- [7/16 @__paleologo] There were things that Astra was proposing that I either didn't understand, or that were not important. I could ask for clarifications. Also, at some point Astra removed some of my original description. But it recalled it and added it back. 7/ --- [8/16 @__paleologo] The final report is about 35 pages long. Years of thinking coming to a conclusion. Qualitative and quantitative productivity improvement. I am not sad at all. Now I can build on this result, or move on to the next problem. 8/ --- [9/16 @__paleologo] Now, one observation. There are lots of Erdös problems being solved. These make the news because they are simple to state, self-contained and long-standing. 9/ --- [10/16 @__paleologo] But out there, there are thousand of people working on dirty engineering problems that intrinsically are not suited to one-shotting or recursive self-improvement. We (the engineers) are the essential experiential link to reality. 10/ --- [11/16 @__paleologo] There *has* to be a dialogue between AI and humans for the next few year. My relationship, at least, is increasingly symbiotic. I am the hermit crab, and Astra is the sea anemone. I decide where to go, but can delegate lots of task. and Astra gets to do cool stuff. 11/ --- [12/16 @__paleologo] But *I* know crowding. *I* know the duration. *I* can screen the relevant variables. And so on. Astra is carrying over tasks, mostly correctly, to conclusion. Solving a problem. It doesn't, couldn't, shouldn't know what is the problem, and what is the final goal. 12/ --- [13/16 @__paleologo] Russell introduced the concepts of "knowledge by acquaintance" vs "knowledge by description". Polanyi introduced the concept of "tacit knowledge". I think that the Dark Matter of Knowledge is "tacit knowledge by acquaintance". 13/ --- [14/16 @__paleologo] It's not spelled out. You have to experience it. And it makes the vast majority of problems we try to solve, as engineers, or empirical beings. World models can't even begin to get there, at least not yet. 14/ --- [15/16 @__paleologo] So, modulo existential accident that will bring the apocalypse, your job is going to be safe for quite a while. No, it's going to be better. Be optimistic. 15/ --- [16/16 @__paleologo] P.S.: I am sure lots of people would be very interested in learning what other people have been doing with dirty engineering problems.
